slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Its own competency questions; we return to each

items: What does a Bitcoin transaction ask full nodes to do?
How is a transaction serialized in the extended and the legacy format?
What do the version, marker and flag tell a node?
Which three meanings has the sequence field carried?
Why did witnesses in the input script make the identifier malleable?
How are weight and vbytes computed, and does 569 reproduce from the bytes?
Who creates new bitcoins, and when can they be spent?

slides.notes: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.

slides.title: Two serializations, two identifiers
slides.sub: Extended with the witness, legacy without it

groups.note: One payment, written twice: with the witness and without.
The legacy form is shorter: no marker, flag or witness.
Different bytes give different hashes, so each form has its own identifier.

items.cap: Python 3.14.6 - ALICE, PREV, FIRST and tx as set up on slide 7

items.body: Result: the two serializations of one payment
The 69-byte difference is the marker, the flag and the witness; only the legacy bytes are hashed for the txid.

slides.notes: The same payment is written twice. The legacy form leaves out marker, flag and witness, and its hash is the txid that explorers show. The extended form has its own hash, the wtxid. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The txid hashes the legacy bytes only; the wtxid hashes everything

slides.title: Ten bitcoins to Hal Finney, block 170
slides.sub: The first transaction ever to spend an output

items.cap: Hal Finney, 1972 - Daily News-Post, public domain

items: WHAT: Satoshi Nakamoto sent Hal Finney 10 bitcoins, the first transaction ever to spend an output.
WHY: Finney had started the software the day before and wanted to test the network with a real payment.
HOW: One input points at the coinbase of block 9; two outputs pay 10 BTC to Finney and 40 BTC back.
SO WHAT: Legacy format, no marker, no flag, no witness: every field this chapter reads was already there.

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto (sender) and Hal Finney, cryptographer and the second person to run the software
items.where: block 170 of the blockchain; Finney's computer in California, running bitcoin since the day before

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2009-01-12. On 11 January 2009 Hal Finney posted two words, running bitcoin, and the next day the software's author sent him 10 BTC. The lesson is that the format you are reading is the one from block 170.

slides.title: Version, marker and flag
slides.sub: Version, marker and flag are the edition number and labels on the envelope.

items.label: The version field
items.sub: Four bytes that say which rule edition applies. Like the edition number printed on a form.

items.label: The marker and the flag
items.sub: Two bytes that announce the witness format. Like a fragile label on a parcel.

slides.notes: The first six bytes of a transaction are not data about money. They tell a node which rules apply and whether a witness follows, so every later field is read correctly.

slides.title: Version, marker and flag: concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Version 1
items.meaning: 01000000 in the first four bytes.
items.analogy: edition 1 of a form, still valid in every office.

items.label: Version 2 and BIP68
items.meaning: The version that turns sequence into a timelock.
items.analogy: edition 2, which adds a waiting-period box to the form.

items.label: The version 3 proposal
items.meaning: A policy, not a consensus change.
items.analogy: a draft edition that offices may choose to accept.

items.label: Presigned transactions
items.meaning: Signed now, broadcast years later.
items.analogy: a post-dated cheque kept in a drawer.

items.label: Marker byte
items.meaning: A zero where a count cannot be zero.
items.analogy: a sticker on a parcel saying special contents inside.

items.label: Flag byte
items.meaning: One, with other values reserved.
items.analogy: a second sticker that names the kind of extras.

slides.notes: These cards cover Version 1, Version 2 and BIP68, The version 3 proposal, Presigned transactions, Marker byte and Flag byte. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The first six bytes
slides.sub: Version, marker and flag in Alice's transaction

groups.note: Raw bytes let us address single bytes.
The version takes four bytes, least significant first.
Marker zero and flag one announce a witness.

items.cap: Python 3.14.6 - ALICE, PREV, FIRST and tx as set up on slide 7

items.body: Result: the first six bytes, read
A node that sees a zero where it expects a count knows the extended format is in use.

slides.notes: Six bytes decide how everything after them is read. The version says which rules apply, and the zero marker with the one flag announces a witness. A legacy parser would read the zero as an empty input list. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A zero marker where an input count would be tells old and new nodes apart

slides.title: Inputs
slides.sub: Inputs are the banknotes you hand over, each named by its address.

items.label: The input list
items.sub: The list of coins this transaction spends. Like a receipt listing the notes you hand over.

items.label: The outpoint
items.sub: The address of one coin: a transaction and an output number. Like a street address with building and flat.

items.label: Internal and display byte order
items.sub: The same 32 bytes can be read in two directions. Like a book you can read from the front or the back.

items.label: The input script
items.sub: The slot where legacy inputs put their proof. Like a keyhole that legacy inputs fill with the key.

slides.notes: Inputs name the coins a transaction spends, and they state no amount. We meet the compact count, the outpoint and its two byte orders, and the database of unspent coins.

slides.title: Inputs: concepts (1 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Input count
items.meaning: At least one, in practice a few thousand.
items.analogy: counting how many cheques are stapled to a payment.

items.label: CompactSize unsigned integer
items.meaning: 1, 3, 5 or 9 bytes, by value.
items.analogy: a ticket machine: small numbers get short tickets.

items.label: Other variable-length integers
items.meaning: Three encodings, one name that is safe.
items.analogy: three kinds of ticket sold under one name.

items.label: Outpoint
items.meaning: 36 bytes: a txid and an index.
items.analogy: a street address: building number plus flat number.

items.label: The previous transaction's identifier
items.meaning: The first 32 bytes of an outpoint.
items.analogy: the building number in that address.

slides.notes: These cards cover Input count, CompactSize unsigned integer, Other variable-length integers, Outpoint and The previous transaction's identifier. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: CompactSize: counting in few bytes
slides.sub: The bytes a count takes grow with the count

groups.note: Six counts, chosen where the encoding changes length.
Encode each count and measure the bytes it takes.
A first byte of fd, fe or ff announces a longer number.

items.cap: Python 3.14.6 - ALICE, PREV, FIRST and tx as set up on slide 7

items.body: Result: bytes taken by each count
First bytes written: 01 fc fd fd fe ff. The values fd, fe and ff announce longer numbers.

slides.notes: Counts in a transaction use a variable-length integer. Up to 252 it is one byte; beyond that a first byte of fd, fe or ff says that two, four or eight more bytes follow. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Small counts cost one byte; the first byte warns when a longer number follows

slides.title: Inputs: concepts (2 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Output index
items.meaning: Four bytes counting from zero.
items.analogy: the flat number inside the building, counted from zero.

items.label: The rule against double spending
items.meaning: An output is spent at most once.
items.analogy: a banknote that can be handed over only once.

items.label: Conflicting transactions
items.meaning: Same outpoint, two spenders.
items.analogy: two cheques written against the same banknote.

items.label: The UTXO database
items.meaning: Remove what is spent, add what is created.
items.analogy: a drawer holding only the banknotes nobody has spent.

items.label: Digest
items.meaning: 32 bytes that identify a transaction.
items.analogy: a fingerprint taken from a whole document.

slides.notes: These cards cover Output index, The rule against double spending, Conflicting transactions, The UTXO database and Digest. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6.

slides.title: The outpoint, read both ways round
slides.sub: Which coin an input spends

lines: check = back == stored and shown == txid(PREV)

groups.note: An input names a coin: the earlier txid and an output number.
Explorers print the same 32 bytes in reverse order.
Reversing twice restores the original, and it equals the earlier txid.

items.cap: Python 3.14.6 - ALICE, PREV, FIRST and tx as set up on slide 7

items.body: Result: the first 16 hex digits of the outpoint
Input 0 spends output 1 of the earlier transaction; its stored and printed forms are mirror images.

slides.notes: An input points at a coin by the txid of an earlier transaction and an output number. The bytes are stored in one order and printed in the reverse order, which is a classic source of mistakes. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: An input states no amount; it names a coin by transaction and output number

slides.title: Inputs: concepts (3 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Internal byte order
items.meaning: The order inside the bytes.
items.analogy: reading a phone number from its last digit.

items.label: Display byte order
items.meaning: The order on the screen.
items.analogy: reading the phone number the usual way round.

items.label: Input script
items.meaning: 107 bytes for a legacy spend, 0 for segwit.
items.analogy: the key you hand over at the door.

items.label: Script length prefix
items.meaning: 0x6b says 107 bytes follow.
items.analogy: a label on a box saying how many items it holds.

slides.title: A spend updates the UTXO set
slides.sub: Remove what is spent, add what is created

lines: for i in tx['inputs']:                # spent: out
for n, o in enumerate(tx['outputs']): # new: in

groups.note: Before the payment the set holds Alice's one coin.
Each input removes the coin it names.
Each output adds a new coin, named by txid and position.
What is left over is the fee; no field states it.

items.cap: Python 3.14.6 - ALICE, PREV, FIRST and tx as set up on slide 7

items.body: Result: the set of unspent outputs, before and after
The fee of 5,000 satoshis is not a field; it is 100,000 - 95,000.

slides.notes: A full node keeps a database of unspent outputs. Applying a transaction removes the coins its inputs name and adds the coins its outputs create. The difference in value is the fee. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Nodes keep only unspent outputs; the fee is whatever is left over

slides.title: 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas
slides.sub: The most famous purchase ever made with bitcoin

items.cap: Papa John's plaque - Sanjev Rajaram, CC0

items: WHAT: Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas that a forum user ordered for him.
WHY: He wanted to show that bitcoin could buy something real; his forum offer began four days earlier.
HOW: The payment confirmed in block 57,043: 131 inputs, one output of 10,000 BTC, a fee of 0.99 BTC.
SO WHAT: A wallet that gathered many 50 BTC rewards must list every one of them as an input.

items.who: Laszlo Hanyecz, programmer in Jacksonville, Florida; the pizzas ordered by forum user jercos
items.where: a Papa John's on Atlantic Avenue, Jacksonville - the shop now carries a plaque

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2010-05-22. Four days after offering 10,000 BTC on the bitcointalk forum to anyone who would send him two pizzas, Laszlo Hanyecz reported that the deal was done. The lesson is that an input count of 131 is what one-output payments can look like.

slides.title: The sequence field
slides.sub: The sequence field is a booth ticket whose meaning changed three times.

items.label: Original sequence-based replacement
items.sub: The first use of the field: replace an unfinished transaction. Like an order slip you can reissue until the kitchen closes.

items.label: Opt-in replace-by-fee
items.sub: A later transaction that pays more replaces an earlier one. Like outbidding someone at an auction.

items.label: Sequence as a relative timelock
items.sub: A coin that cannot be spent until some time after it arrived. Like a gift card that activates a week after purchase.

slides.notes: One four-byte field has carried three meanings in fifteen years. We decode it against two proposals, BIP125 and BIP68, and see why bit 31 matters.

slides.title: The sequence field: concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Sequence number
items.meaning: The last four bytes of an input.
items.analogy: a counter on a ticket that the booth can reissue.

items.label: Setup and refund transactions
items.meaning: A deposit that needs both signatures.
items.analogy: a locked deposit box that needs two keys.

items.label: Payment channel
items.meaning: Many versions, one broadcast.
items.analogy: a bar tab: many orders, one bill at the end.

items.label: The replacement bandwidth attack
items.meaning: 20 KB in, 10 GB out, every minute.
items.analogy: refiling the same form again and again to clog the office.

items.label: Opt-in replace-by-fee
items.meaning: A higher fee rate replaces a lower one.
items.analogy: a form that says I may be replaced by a better-paid one.

slides.notes: These cards cover Sequence number, Setup and refund transactions, Payment channel, The replacement bandwidth attack and Opt-in replace-by-fee. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Four sequence values, three meanings
slides.sub: Final, replaceable, and a relative timelock

groups.note: Four values: final, almost final, replaceable, thirty blocks.
The decoder applies BIP68 and BIP125, which reused the field.
Each row shows the replace signal and the relative timelock.

items.cap: Python 3.14.6 - ALICE, PREV, FIRST and tx as set up on slide 7

items.body: Result: four values decoded
The first two are final or almost final; the third signals replacement; only the last carries a timelock.

slides.notes: The same four bytes signal finality, opt-in replacement under BIP125 and a relative timelock under BIP68. Setting bit 31 switches the timelock off, which is why the third value shows none. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Bit 31 of the sequence field is the security bit of this chapter

slides.title: The sequence field: concepts (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: The BIP125 signal
items.meaning: Below 0xfffffffe means replaceable.
items.analogy: a tick box marked amendable on the form.

items.label: BIP68 relative timelock
items.meaning: 30 blocks: confirm 29 blocks after the output.
items.analogy: a coupon valid only some days after purchase.

items.label: The type flag
items.meaning: Bit 22 chooses blocks or 512-second units.
items.analogy: a switch choosing between counting turns and counting minutes.

items.label: The disable flag
items.meaning: Bit 31 switches the timelock off.
items.analogy: an off switch that makes the coupon valid at once.

items.label: The 16-bit mask
items.meaning: 65,535 blocks or units, about a year.
items.analogy: a counter with room for only 65,535 ticks.

slides.notes: These cards cover The BIP125 signal, BIP68 relative timelock, The type flag, The disable flag and The 16-bit mask. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6.

slides.sub: How two huge outputs added up to a negative number

items.body: Result: the arithmetic of block 74,638

slides.notes: In August 2010 a block carried two outputs of about 92 billion bitcoins each. Their sum wrapped around to a negative number, which passed the check on the total. Checking every output closes the hole. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.title: The block that created 184 billion bitcoins
slides.sub: A bug that created money out of thin air

items.cap: Satoshi bust, Budapest - Fekist, CC BY-SA 4.0

items: WHAT: Block 74,638 held a transaction with two outputs of 92 billion bitcoins each, 184 billion in all.
WHY: Added as 64-bit integers the amounts wrapped to a small negative number, which passed the check.
HOW: Jeff Garzik reported it within two hours; Satoshi patched it in about five; the chain recovered at block 74,691.
SO WHAT: Bitcoin Core still cites the bug, CVE-2010-5139, in tx_check.cpp.

items.who: an unknown attacker; Jeff Garzik, who reported the strange block on the forum; Satoshi Nakamoto, who patched the software the same day
items.where: block 74,638 - and the bitcointalk forum thread Strange block 74638, where the fix was coordinated within hours

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2010-08-15. Block 74,638 contained a transaction with two outputs of 92,233,720,368.54277039 BTC each. The lesson is that a signed amount needs a range check; the chain learned it the hard way.

slides.title: Dust limits by output type
slides.sub: The smallest output a node will relay

lines: for s in (P2PKH, P2WPKH, P2TR, RET)]

groups.note: Four scripts: three that can be spent and one data carrier.
The limit is the cost to create plus spend, at the relay fee.
Segwit outputs cost less to spend; OP_RETURN is never dust.

items.cap: Python 3.14.6 - ALICE, PREV, FIRST and tx as set up on slide 7

items.body: Result: dust limit in satoshis, at 3,000 sat/kvB
An output below its limit is not relayed. OP_RETURN outputs cannot be spent, so their limit is zero.

slides.notes: An output is dust when it costs more to spend than it is worth, at the relay fee. Segwit outputs are cheaper to spend, so their limit is lower. A data-carrier output can never be spent and is exempt. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Dust is a policy about who pays for the UTXO set: everyone, for ever

slides.title: Witnesses
slides.sub: A witness is the ID you show at the counter, kept off the receipt.

items.label: The idea of a witness
items.sub: Evidence that the spender may spend, kept apart. Like the ID card you show at the counter.

items.label: The malleability problems
items.sub: Changing a transaction's identifier without changing what it pays. Like re-spelling a name so the filing clerk loses the receipt.

items.label: Segregated witness
items.sub: The upgrade that moved the proof out of the identifier. Like keeping the passport photo off the ticket number.

items.label: Witness structure serialization
items.sub: How the separate proofs are written after the main fields. Like annex pages bound behind the main letter.

slides.notes: A witness is the proof that a spender may spend. We see how proofs inside the input script made identifiers malleable, and how segregated witness repaired that as a soft fork.

items.analogy: needing the key to get the key.

items.analogy: a stranger rewording your cheque without changing the sum.

items.analogy: four ways to write the same number in words.

slides.title: Segwit: change the witness, keep the txid
slides.sub: What the two identifiers cover

The txid ignores the witness, so it stays.
The wtxid covers the witness, so it changes.

Only the wtxid notices the new witness; the txid, and everything built on it, stays valid.

slides.title: Mt. Gox blames malleability
slides.sub: An exchange blames the protocol, and researchers check

items.cap: Mt. Gox logo - author unknown, public domain

items: WHAT: Mt. Gox halted withdrawals and blamed transaction malleability for missing bitcoins.
WHY: A stranger can re-encode an input script, change the txid and make a payment look as if it failed.
HOW: Decker and Wattenhofer of ETH Zurich recorded a year of traffic: only 1,811 BTC were hit before the press release.
SO WHAT: Segregated witness took the input script out of the txid in 2017.

items.who: Mt. Gox, then the largest bitcoin exchange, and its CEO Mark Karpeles; Christian Decker and Roger Wattenhofer of ETH Zurich, who measured the claim
items.where: Shibuya, Tokyo - and the whole Bitcoin network, whose relayed transactions the researchers recorded

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2014-02-10. On 7 February 2014 Mt. Gox halted bitcoin withdrawals, and on 10 February it issued a press release blaming a bug in the bitcoin software: someone could alter transaction details to make it seem that a sending of bitcoins had not occurred when it had.

slides.title: Hard fork or soft fork?
slides.sub: Why segregated witness could be activated without splitting the network

left.head: A hard fork loosens the rules
rows: Blocks that old nodes reject become valid.
Every node must upgrade, or the chain splits.
Like a new road standard that old cars cannot use.

right.head: A soft fork tightens the rules
rows: New nodes reject more; they accept nothing new.
Old nodes still follow the chain and accept its blocks.
Like a stricter speed limit that old cars can still obey.

slides.notes: Segregated witness was a soft fork. Old nodes saw the new outputs as anyone-can-spend scripts and accepted the blocks, while upgraded nodes enforced the witness rules. That is why it could be activated without a split.
slides.take: A soft fork can only restrict; old nodes keep accepting the blocks

slides.title: Lock time and the coinbase
slides.sub: A lock time is a post-dated cheque; a coinbase is the mint's wage slip.

items.label: Lock time
items.sub: A rule that a transaction may not enter a block before a time. Like a post-dated cheque.

items.label: Coinbase transactions
items.sub: The first transaction of every block, which creates new coins. Like the mint's wage slip for the miner.

slides.notes: Two special cases of a transaction: one that may not be mined before a time, and one that creates new coins. The clock and the money supply both follow from simple rules.

slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: The lock time field

items.analogy: a do-not-open-before date on an envelope.

items.label: Lock time as a block height

items.analogy: do not open before a numbered page of the logbook.

items.label: Lock time as an epoch time
items.meaning: 500,000,000 or more is a timestamp.
items.analogy: do not open before this calendar date.

items.label: Median time past
items.meaning: The middle of eleven block times.
items.analogy: asking the middle voter, not the loudest.

items.label: Coinbase transaction
items.meaning: First in the block, made by the miner.
items.analogy: the bonus the mint pays whoever closes the page.

slides.title: Lock time and the median time past
slides.sub: Which clock a lock time is read against

lines: times = [1675556500 + 100 * k for k in ks]

groups.note: Eleven block times, out of order, as on the real chain.
Median time past is the middle of the eleven, not the newest.
Small values are heights; large values are times.

items.cap: Python 3.14.6 - ALICE, PREV, FIRST and tx as set up on slide 7

items.body: Result: block times in seconds after 1675556500
The median of the eleven is 2,100 s, which is 600 s below the highest timestamp. Lock time kinds: any block, block height, epoch time.

slides.notes: Block timestamps are not monotonic, so a time lock is compared with the median of the last eleven. Values below 500 million are heights; larger ones are times. The median lags the highest timestamp. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Lock time says not before; nothing in a transaction says not after

slides.title: Weight and foundations
slides.sub: Weight is a transaction's postage; foundations are the post office's rules.

items.label: Weight and vbytes
items.sub: The measure that decides how much block space a transaction uses. Like postage that charges less for the small print.

items.label: Foundations
items.sub: The hashes, identifiers and rule sets the chapter rests on. Like the foundations under a house.

slides.title: How a txid is made
slides.sub: Double SHA-256 of the legacy bytes, reversed

groups.note: Start from the legacy bytes: no witness.
Hash them twice with SHA-256, one hash after the other.
Reverse the digest for display: that is the txid.

items.cap: Python 3.14.6 - ALICE, PREV, FIRST and tx as set up on slide 7

items.body: Result: from the legacy bytes to the txid
The reversed digest equals the library's txid.

slides.notes: A txid is not a field. It is the double SHA-256 of the legacy serialization, shown in reverse byte order. We recompute it from the bytes and it matches the library and the explorer. It is example 18 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Identifiers are computed, never stored: anyone can recompute them

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per part, each provable from its slides

items: A transaction asks strangers to update their ledgers: inputs point, witnesses prove, outputs assign.
The sequence field has meant three things, and the lock time is read against the median of eleven blocks.
An output is an amount and a condition; the fee is a difference, and dust is a policy about everyone's database.
Witnesses in the input script made identifiers malleable; segregated witness moved them out, as a soft fork.
The coinbase creates coins under a schedule that ends at block 6,929,999, and weight is what a block is filled by.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature, one for each group of parts. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page lets you rerun all eighteen examples.
